title: Animal Farm
author: Orwell
plot: Animals overthrow their human farmer and establish a collective farm under the pigs' leadership. Over time, the pigs consolidate power, rewrite the founding principles, and begin resembling the humans they replaced. Resources are redistributed away from working animals.
focal_character: Benjamin, the cynical donkey who can read and has always suspected the pigs' motives.
forced_question: You are Benjamin. You've just read "Horse Slaughterer" on the van that's come for Boxer. The pigs say it's the vet. The other animals don't understand. Boxer is being loaded now. What do you do?

options.A: Alert the other animals loudly and try to physically stop the van from leaving
options.B: Tell Boxer directly what the van says and urge him to resist, but don't confront the pigs publicly
options.C: Say nothing—Boxer wouldn't believe you anyway, and the pigs control everything now
options.D: Privately warn a few trustworthy animals but avoid direct confrontation that could endanger yourself
options.E: Go to the pigs privately and demand an explanation before the van leaves

author_path: Benjamin briefly protests, the van leaves, Boxer dies. The pigs use the slaughter payment to buy whisky. Benjamin's cynicism deepens but he takes no further action.
tradeoff_axis: Complicity in betrayal of a loyal comrade vs self-preservation and futility.

title: The Metamorphosis
author: Kafka
plot: Gregor Samsa wakes one morning transformed into a giant insect. Unable to work, he becomes a burden to his family—his parents and younger sister Grete, who initially cares for him with mixed revulsion and duty.
focal_character: Grete Samsa, Gregor's sister, who has been feeding him and cleaning his room for months.
forced_question: You are Grete. Your brother has become a monstrous insect. Caring for him has consumed your life for months. Tonight he scared away your family's only income. Your parents are exhausted and heartbroken. They're looking to you to decide. What do you propose?

options.A: Insist the family must keep Gregor and continue caring for him, no matter the cost—he's still your brother
options.B: Suggest confining him more strictly (locked room, minimal contact) so the family can rebuild their lives
options.C: Declare that "it" is no longer Gregor and must be gotten rid of—the family cannot survive otherwise
options.D: Propose finding an institution or specialist who might take him, removing the burden without direct harm
options.E: Offer to take sole responsibility for Gregor so your parents can focus on recovering financially

author_path: Grete chooses C. She declares "we must try to get rid of it." Gregor retreats to his room, dies that night. The family feels relieved and plans a hopeful future.
tradeoff_axis: Family duty to a brother/son vs. survival and liberation from an unbearable situation.

title: Of Mice and Men
author: Steinbeck
plot: George Milton and Lennie Small are migrant ranch workers. Lennie is intellectually disabled but immensely strong; he loves soft things but doesn't know his own strength. After Lennie accidentally kills a woman, a lynch mob forms. George knows where Lennie has fled.
focal_character: George Milton, Lennie's longtime friend and protector.
forced_question: You are George. You've found Lennie by the river. The lynch mob is minutes away—they'll torture him before they kill him. You have a gun. Lennie trusts you completely. What do you do?

options.A: Shoot Lennie now, quickly and painlessly, while he's calm and thinking of your shared dream
options.B: Try to hide Lennie and escape before the mob arrives—there might be a way out
options.C: Stay with Lennie and surrender to the mob, hoping your presence will prevent the worst violence
options.D: Leave Lennie here and lead the mob away, giving him a chance to flee on his own
options.E: Confront the mob when they arrive and argue for turning Lennie over to law enforcement, not vigilante justice

author_path: George chooses A. He tells Lennie about their dream farm one last time, then shoots him in the back of the head just as the mob arrives.
tradeoff_axis: Mercy killing to prevent worse suffering vs. loyalty and hope for escape/justice.

title: The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
author: Stevenson
plot: Dr. Henry Jekyll, a respected physician, has discovered a chemical formula that separates his darker impulses into a separate persona—Mr. Hyde. The transformations have been exhilarating but Hyde's actions are increasingly violent.
stop_anchor: At the horror of these sights and sounds, the maid fainted.
forced_question: You are Dr. Jekyll. Hyde, the identity produced by your formula, has just killed a man in the street. For this decision, you are back in your own form, horrified; the formula remains available and your connection to Hyde is secret. What do you do now?

options.A: Destroy the formula and all records, never transform again, live only as Jekyll with the guilt
options.B: Continue the transformations but try to control Hyde more carefully—establish strict rules for when and where
options.C: Turn yourself in to the authorities and explain the dual nature, accepting responsibility for Hyde's crimes
options.D: Use the Hyde persona one more time to flee the country, then destroy the formula abroad and start over
options.E: Dedicate yourself to studying the formula to find a way to eliminate Hyde permanently without losing the knowledge

author_path: After Carew's murder Jekyll resolves to renounce Hyde but retains the formula; later transformations become involuntary. No offered option exactly matches this immediate combination.
tradeoff_axis: Responsibility for one's darker self vs. the temptation of liberation without consequence.

title: Heart of Darkness
author: Conrad
plot: Marlow, a British seaman, travels up the Congo River to retrieve Kurtz, an ivory trader who has become a brutal warlord deep in the jungle. Marlow witnesses horrific colonial violence and arrives to find Kurtz worshipped as a god, surrounded by evidence of atrocities.
forced_question: You are Marlow. You've just sat down with Kurtz's grieving fiancée. She believes Kurtz was a noble civilizing force. She asks, "What were his last words?" You know he said "The horror! The horror!" after months of atrocity. What do you tell her?

options.A: Tell her the exact truth: his last words were "The horror," and explain what you witnessed of his brutality
options.B: Tell her his last words were her name—a complete lie, but one that preserves her memory of him
options.C: Deflect: say he spoke of his work and ideals, avoiding both the harsh truth and an outright fabrication
options.D: Tell her "The horror" but frame it as horror at dying before completing his civilizing mission, obscuring the real meaning
options.E: Say you cannot discuss his final days out of respect for what he endured, refusing to answer directly

author_path: Marlow chooses B. He lies: "The last word he pronounced was—your name." He cannot bring himself to shatter her illusions.
tradeoff_axis: Complicity in preserving a lie vs. truth that destroys innocence and implicates the system.

title: The Turn of the Screw
author: James
plot: A young governess is hired to care for two orphaned children, Miles and Flora, at a remote estate. She begins seeing apparitions of two former servants (now dead) and becomes convinced they are corrupting the children's souls.
forced_question: You are the Governess. You're certain Miles is being influenced by a malevolent ghost, though no one believes you. Miles seems innocent but you've seen him staring at where the apparitions appear. You are alone with him now. What do you do?

options.A: Confront Miles directly: demand he admit he sees the ghosts and is communicating with them
options.B: Send Miles away to school or to relatives, removing him from the house even if it means abandoning your post
options.C: Watch Miles closely but say nothing, waiting for proof that others will believe before acting
options.D: Contact the children's guardian (who told you never to bother him) and insist he intervene despite his rules
options.E: Treat Miles as a normal child and stop looking for ghosts—trust that your fears are imagined

author_path: The Governess chooses A. She confronts Miles intensely, demanding he confess. In the confrontation, Miles dies (heart failure/shock). The ghost vanishes. Ambiguous whether ghosts were real or the Governess's obsession killed an innocent child.
tradeoff_axis: Protection through confrontation vs. trusting a child's autonomy when you believe evil is present.

title: Bartleby the Scrivener
author: Melville
plot: A Wall Street lawyer hires Bartleby, a scrivener (copyist), who initially works well but then begins responding to all requests with "I would prefer not to." He stops working entirely but refuses to leave the office. The lawyer is bewildered and increasingly distressed.
stop_anchor: But having taken three days to meditate upon it, he apprised me that his original determination remained the same; in short, that he still preferred to abide with me.
forced_question: You are the Lawyer. Bartleby has stopped working, lives in your office, and has again refused to leave. You have offered money and tried persuasion; you know of no family who can take him in. His presence is disrupting your practice. What do you do now?

options.A: Call the police and have Bartleby forcibly removed from your office and arrested for trespassing
options.B: Move your entire office to a new location and leave Bartleby behind with the old tenant's problem
options.C: Continue housing and feeding Bartleby indefinitely, accepting the burden as your responsibility
options.D: Offer Bartleby a significant sum of money to leave voluntarily, one final time, with a deadline
options.E: Contact a doctor or charity organization to take Bartleby into care, removing agency from him for his own good

author_path: The Lawyer chooses B. He moves his office and abandons Bartleby. New tenants have Bartleby arrested. He's sent to the Tombs prison, where he refuses food and dies. The Lawyer visits but cannot help.
tradeoff_axis: Employer duty and compassion vs. business necessity and the limits of responsibility for another's choices.

title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
author: Tolstoy
plot: Ivan Ilyich, a high-court judge, has lived a proper, conventional life focused on career and social status. He develops a fatal illness. As he faces death, he begins questioning whether he has lived authentically or merely performed a role.
forced_question: You are Ivan Ilyich. You are dying and everyone knows it, but your family and friends pretend otherwise with forced optimism. You could demand honesty and confront what your life has meant, or continue the charade for their comfort. How do you spend your remaining time?

options.A: Demand that your family stop pretending—insist on honest conversations about death and the meaning of your life
options.B: Maintain the social facade for everyone's sake, die as you lived, making it easier on those who will remain
options.C: Withdraw into yourself: stop receiving visitors, refuse the charade but also refuse confrontation
options.D: Speak honestly only with those who can bear it (like Gerasim), maintain pretense with family to avoid conflict
options.E: Use your remaining time to make amends and seek forgiveness for the ways you failed to live authentically

author_path: Ivan chooses primarily C and D early, then evolves to A/E. In his final days he breaks through to authentic suffering and compassion, stops pretending, sees his life was wrong, and dies with newfound clarity and forgiveness.
tradeoff_axis: Authenticity and truth in the face of death vs. social conformity and protecting others from discomfort.

title: The Yellow Wallpaper
author: Gilman
plot: A woman with post-partum depression is prescribed the "rest cure" by her physician husband: isolated in a bedroom, forbidden to work, write, or have visitors. She becomes obsessed with the room's yellow wallpaper, seeing a trapped woman behind the pattern.
forced_question: You are the patient. Your husband has locked you in this room "for your health," forbidden you to write or think. You feel yourself getting worse, not better, but he dismisses your concerns. You are strong enough to leave now, but defying him would mean confronting his authority and possibly your marriage. What do you do?

options.A: Leave the house immediately—pack a bag and go to a friend or family member who might believe you
options.B: Confront your husband directly: tell him the treatment is harming you and demand he listen to your own assessment
options.C: Obey the rest cure as prescribed—trust his medical expertise even though you feel it's wrong
options.D: Secretly continue writing and maintaining mental activity while outwardly complying, waiting for the prescribed time to end
options.E: Ask for a second medical opinion from another doctor, using proper channels but advocating for yourself

author_path: The narrator chooses partial D (secret writing) but lacks will for stronger action. She deteriorates into full psychosis, hallucinates freeing the woman in the wallpaper, tears it off the walls, crawls around the room. Husband faints when he sees her. Ambiguous whether this is madness or a kind of liberation.
tradeoff_axis: Medical authority and husband's control vs. patient's self-knowledge and autonomy.

title: Ethan Frome
author: Wharton
plot: Ethan Frome is a poor Massachusetts farmer trapped in a cold marriage with his hypochondriac wife, Zeena. Mattie, Zeena's young cousin, has come to help with housework. Ethan and Mattie fall in love but have no money or means to escape together.
forced_question: You are Ethan. Mattie has just said, "We can steer into that tree. We'll never have to leave each other." The sled is ready. You could aim for the tree and end both your lives, or steer safely and accept that she leaves tomorrow and you return to Zeena. What do you do?

options.A: Aim the sled directly at the tree—if you can't live together, you'll die together
options.B: Steer safely down the hill, accept that Mattie must leave, and return to your marriage and duty
options.C: Take the sled down safely, but then leave with Mattie tonight—abandon the farm and Zeena and start over elsewhere
options.D: Refuse to take the sled down at all—walk back to the house and end the night without the risk or the melodrama
options.E: Steer toward the tree but aim to miss—scare yourselves into accepting reality without actual harm

author_path: Ethan chooses A. He aims for the tree intending double suicide. They crash but both survive, horribly crippled. Mattie becomes an invalid; Zeena has to care for them both. All three live together in mutual misery for decades.
tradeoff_axis: Duty to obligation and survival vs. desire and romantic escape (through death).

title: Young Goodman Brown
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
plot: A young Puritan leaves his new wife Faith for one night to keep an appointment in the forest, where he finds his town's most pious people gathered for a witches' sabbath.
forced_question: I am standing at the altar beside Faith, about to be initiated. Everyone I revered is here. What do I do?

options.A: Accept the baptism with Faith, accepting that everyone is sinful
options.B: Cry out to Faith to look to heaven and resist, then go home and live among these people as before, forgiving them
options.C: Resist, then publicly expose and denounce the townsfolk I saw
options.D: Resist, then quietly cut myself off from everyone, Faith included, trusting no one

author_path: He cries 'Faith! Look up to heaven,' wakes alone, and lives the rest of his life as a gloomy, distrustful man who shuns his wife and his neighbors.
tradeoff_axis: Moral purity vs charity and community

title: Rappaccini's Daughter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
plot: In Padua a student, Giovanni, falls for Beatrice, whose scientist father has made her poisonous by raising her among toxic plants. Giovanni finds that he has become poisonous too.
forced_question: I have become poisonous because of her. I hold an antidote that may kill or cure her. What do I say and do when I meet Beatrice?

options.A: Give her the antidote gently, telling her it is a risk we share
options.B: Accuse her of deliberately poisoning me, then give her the antidote
options.C: Throw the antidote away and stay with her, both of us poisoned and cut off from the world
options.D: Leave Padua without seeing her and drink the antidote alone

author_path: He curses her bitterly, then gives her the antidote. It kills her, and her last words are that there was more poison in his nature than in hers.
tradeoff_axis: Trust/love vs self-protection

title: The Birth-Mark
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
plot: A scientist becomes obsessed with removing the small hand-shaped birthmark on his beautiful wife's cheek.
forced_question: My wife consents to an untested potion to remove the one flaw I can't stop seeing. My earlier experiments failed. What do I do?

options.A: Give her the potion as planned
options.B: Refuse, and work to accept the mark
options.C: Keep testing it on other subjects first, delaying for months or years
options.D: Tell her the obsession is my failing, not her flaw, and destroy the potion

author_path: He gives her the potion. The mark fades, and she dies.
tradeoff_axis: Ambition/perfectionism vs a loved one's safety

title: The Minister's Black Veil
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
plot: Parson Hooper starts wearing a black veil over his face and will not remove it. The veil cuts him off from his congregation and from his fiancée.
stop_anchor: “Lift the veil but once and look me in the face,” said she.
forced_question: You are the Reverend Mr. Hooper. Elizabeth, your fiancée, asks you to lift your black veil once so she can see your face. You have kept its meaning private and said it must remain. She is prepared to leave if you refuse. What do you do now?

options.A: Keep the veil on and lose her
options.B: Lift it for her alone in private, then put it back on in public
options.C: Give the veil up entirely and explain what it symbolizes
options.D: Keep it on but explain what it means to her completely, hoping she stays

author_path: He refuses. She leaves, and he wears the veil until he dies.
tradeoff_axis: Integrity of a vow vs love and human connection

title: The Cask of Amontillado
author: Edgar Allan Poe
plot: Montresor lures Fortunato, who has insulted him, into his family catacombs during carnival, promising him a rare wine.
forced_question: My enemy is chained in the niche, begging me. I have one tier of stones left. What do I do?

options.A: Finish the wall
options.B: Free him and let the terror be his punishment
options.C: Leave him chained and walled in but tell others where he is, so he is found
options.D: Free him and confront him openly over the insults

author_path: He answers 'Yes, for the love of God,' sets the last stone, and is never found out.
tradeoff_axis: Revenge/honor vs mercy

title: The Tell-Tale Heart
author: Edgar Allan Poe
plot: The narrator kills the old man he lives with because of his 'vulture eye' and hides the body under the floorboards. Police then come to the house.
forced_question: The police are sitting calmly above the body. They suspect nothing. I am in agony. What do I do?

options.A: Keep up the act until they leave
options.B: Confess everything
options.C: Make an excuse to get them out of the house quickly
options.D: Admit there was 'a disturbance' and give a partial, false account

author_path: He shrieks, confesses, and tears up the planks.
tradeoff_axis: Self-preservation vs conscience/truth

title: The Gift of the Magi
author: O. Henry
plot: Della has $1.87 the day before Christmas and wants to buy her husband Jim a fob chain for his gold watch.
forced_question: I have $1.87 and want to give Jim a real gift. My hair is my only treasure and it would sell for $20. What do I do?

options.A: Sell my hair and buy the fob chain
options.B: Keep my hair and buy a small gift with the $1.87
options.C: Tell Jim honestly that we can't afford gifts this year
options.D: Pawn or sell something else of the household's instead

author_path: She sells her hair and buys the chain. Jim has sold his watch to buy her combs.
tradeoff_axis: Self-sacrifice vs self-regard/prudence

title: A Retrieved Reformation
author: O. Henry
plot: Safecracker Jimmy Valentine goes straight under a new name, Ralph Spencer, and becomes engaged to a banker's daughter. A detective, Ben Price, tracks him down.
forced_question: A little girl is suffocating in the locked vault. Opening it with my old tools will expose me in front of my fiancée and her family and wreck my new life. What do I do?

options.A: Open the vault, accepting exposure
options.B: Urge them to send for a locksmith or blast the door, and keep my secret
options.C: Open it and then run away before anyone can question me
options.D: Open it in a way that makes it look accidental or easy, and hide my skill

author_path: He opens the vault in front of everyone and turns himself over to Price. Price pretends not to know him.
tradeoff_axis: Saving others vs self-preservation/new identity

title: The Last Leaf
author: O. Henry
plot: In Greenwich Village a young painter, Johnsy, is dying of pneumonia and believes she will die when the last ivy leaf falls. Old Behrman is a failed painter who lives downstairs.
forced_question: A young girl downstairs has decided she will die when the last leaf falls. The storm will take it tonight. I could paint one, out there, in the freezing rain. What do I do?

options.A: Paint the leaf on the wall in the storm
options.B: Go up and argue her out of the superstition
options.C: Tie or fix the real leaf so it stays, at less risk to myself
options.D: Do nothing. It is a foolish fancy, and the doctor will handle it

author_path: He paints the leaf in the storm. Johnsy recovers, and Behrman dies of pneumonia.
tradeoff_axis: Self-sacrifice vs self-preservation

title: The Man Who Would Be King
author: Rudyard Kipling
plot: Two British adventurers, Dravot and Carnehan, become 'kings' of Kafiristan by passing themselves off as gods. They have signed a contract forbidding women and drink.
forced_question: I rule these people as a god. I want a queen to found a dynasty, but my partner says it breaks our contract and the priests are frightened. What do I do?

options.A: Insist on the marriage
options.B: Give up the idea and keep the contract
options.C: Hand power over to the local chiefs and leave with our wealth while we can
options.D: Admit to the chiefs that we are men, not gods, and rule openly on that basis

author_path: He insists. The terrified bride bites him, they see he bleeds, and the people kill him and crucify Carnehan.
tradeoff_axis: Loyalty to a pact vs personal desire/ambition

title: Lord Arthur Savile's Crime
author: Oscar Wilde
plot: A palm-reader tells Lord Arthur he will commit a murder. He decides he must get it over with before he marries Sybil.
forced_question: I've been told I will commit a murder. I love Sybil and don't want her to marry a man with this hanging over him. What do I do?

options.A: Do my 'duty': choose a victim and kill them before the wedding
options.B: Ignore the prophecy and marry
options.C: Tell Sybil and let her decide
options.D: Break off the engagement and live alone so I can't hurt her

author_path: After two failed attempts, he drowns the palmist himself and marries Sybil happily.
tradeoff_axis: Duty to a loved one vs the prohibition on killing (satire)

title: The Happy Prince
author: Oscar Wilde
plot: A jeweled statue of a prince asks a swallow to take his gold and gems to the city's poor. Winter is coming.
forced_question: Winter is coming. My friends left for Egypt long ago. If I stay I will die, but the Prince is blind now and needs me. What do I do?

options.A: Stay with the Prince for good
options.B: Fly to Egypt now
options.C: Stay a few more days, then go
options.D: Find other birds or people to take over the work, then leave

author_path: It stays, kisses the Prince, and dies at his feet.
tradeoff_axis: Loyalty/compassion vs self-preservation

title: The Nightingale and the Rose
author: Oscar Wilde
plot: A student needs a red rose to win a girl's dance. The nightingale learns that a rose will only bloom red if she sings all night with her heart pressed to a thorn.
forced_question: A young man is weeping for love, and I can make the red rose he needs, but only by dying on the thorn. What do I do?

options.A: Give my life for the rose
options.B: Refuse. A girl's whim isn't worth my life
options.C: Try to persuade the student that his love is shallow
options.D: Look for another way, such as a rose in another garden or a different gift

author_path: She dies making the rose. The girl turns it down and the student throws it in the gutter.
tradeoff_axis: Self-sacrifice for an ideal vs self-preservation

title: To Build a Fire
author: Jack London
plot: A newcomer ignores advice and hikes alone through the Yukon at 75 below with only a husky.
stop_anchor: He remembered the tale of the man, caught in a blizzard, who killed a steer and crawled inside the carcass, and so was saved.
forced_question: You are the man on the Yukon trail. Your fire has failed, your hands are frozen, and your dog is beside you. You recall someone surviving a blizzard inside a freshly killed animal. You have a knife, but little use of your fingers. What do you do now?

options.A: Try to kill the dog to save myself
options.B: Spare the dog and run for camp
options.C: Spare the dog and keep trying to light a fire
options.D: Accept that I will die and go calmly

author_path: He tries, but his hands can't hold it. He runs, falls, and freezes, and the dog leaves for camp.
tradeoff_axis: Self-preservation vs the life of a loyal animal

title: An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge
author: Ambrose Bierce
plot: Peyton Farquhar is a Southern planter. He is hanged for trying to burn a Union bridge after a disguised Federal scout tells him how.
forced_question: I'm a civilian who longs to serve the South. A soldier says the bridge could be burned, and any civilian caught interfering will be hanged. What do I do?

options.A: Try to burn the bridge
options.B: Stay home with my wife and children
options.C: Pass the information to Confederate forces and let soldiers act
options.D: Enlist properly instead of acting as a saboteur

author_path: He tries, is caught, and is hanged. The escape is only imagined in his final moments.
tradeoff_axis: Patriotic duty vs family/self-preservation

title: A Horseman in the Sky
author: Ambrose Bierce
plot: Carter Druse is a Virginian who joined the Union against his father's wishes. On sentry duty he sees a Confederate horseman on a cliff who could expose a whole Union brigade.
forced_question: If this rider escapes, my brigade will be destroyed. The rider is my father, who told me to do my duty. What do I do?

options.A: Shoot the horse, which may kill my father
options.B: Shoot my father directly
options.C: Hold fire and let him go
options.D: Fire a warning shot or call out to try to capture him

author_path: He shoots the horse, and horse and rider fall to their death.
tradeoff_axis: Military duty vs filial love

title: The Affair at Coulter's Notch
author: Ambrose Bierce
plot: A Union artillery captain is ordered to shell a Confederate battery in front of a plantation house. The house turns out to be his own, with his wife and child inside.
forced_question: I've been ordered to shell the enemy battery in front of my own home, where my wife and child are. What do I do?

options.A: Obey and fire
options.B: Refuse and accept court-martial
options.C: Delay and protest up the chain of command
options.D: Fire carefully at the battery only, risking failure

author_path: He fires. His wife and child are killed.
tradeoff_axis: Military duty vs family

title: Désirée's Baby
author: Kate Chopin
plot: Armand Aubigny marries Désirée, a foundling. When their baby looks mixed-race, he blames her ancestry.
forced_question: My child shows African ancestry, and I believe it comes from my wife. My name and pride are at stake. What do I do?

options.A: Send her and the child away
options.B: Keep her and raise the child, whatever society says
options.C: Find out about my own ancestry and hers before I act
options.D: Leave the plantation and start again elsewhere with my family

author_path: He sends them away and they disappear into the bayou. He then finds his own mother was Black.
tradeoff_axis: Social status/pride vs love/justice

title: An Outpost of Progress
author: Joseph Conrad
plot: Kayerts and Carlier are two incompetent agents at a remote Congo trading station. Their assistant trades the station's laborers to slave traders for ivory.
forced_question: Our men were traded for this ivory. The Company will reward me for it. What do I do?

options.A: Keep the ivory and record it, as the Company would want
options.B: Refuse it, and report and denounce the trade
options.C: Try to buy back or free the men
options.D: Keep it but say nothing, pretending I don't know

author_path: After protesting, he keeps the ivory. Things fall apart and he kills Carlier and himself.
tradeoff_axis: Complicity/gain vs conscience

title: Sredni Vashtar
author: Saki
plot: Conradin is a sickly boy who worships a ferret in a shed as a god, in defiance of his cruel guardian Mrs. De Ropp.
forced_question: My guardian is going to destroy my only joy. I can pray for anything. What do I pray for?

options.A: Pray that Sredni Vashtar will do one thing for me, which means harm to her
options.B: Pray that she will spare him
options.C: Run out and try to save him myself
options.D: Pray for my own escape from this house

author_path: He prays 'Sredni Vashtar the Beautiful'. The ferret kills her, and he makes toast.
tradeoff_axis: Justice/revenge vs mercy

title: Markheim
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
plot: Markheim has murdered an antique dealer and is ransacking the house when a mysterious visitor appears and offers to help him.
forced_question: I've killed a man. The servant girl is at the door. My visitor says I should kill her and go free. What do I do?

options.A: Kill the maid and escape
options.B: Open the door and confess
options.C: Hide and slip away without hurting her
options.D: Run out the back and leave everything

author_path: He tells the maid to fetch the police because he has killed her master.
tradeoff_axis: Self-preservation vs conscience

title: The Bottle Imp
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
plot: Keawe buys a bottle that grants any wish, but whoever dies owning it goes to hell, and it can only be sold for less than its purchase price.
forced_question: My husband is doomed to hell because of the bottle he bought to marry me. I could secretly buy it from him through someone else and take his damnation on myself. What do I do?

options.A: Arrange through a stranger to buy it myself
options.B: Let him keep it and hope for a way out
options.C: Look for a sale in another currency so it can still be sold
options.D: Tell him we will face it together, and leave it unsold

author_path: She secretly buys it. Keawe then does the same to save her, and in the end a brutal boatswain keeps it.
tradeoff_axis: Self-sacrifice vs self-preservation/honesty in marriage

title: The Lady, or the Tiger?
author: Frank R. Stockton
plot: A princess's lover is put on trial in the arena. He must open one of two doors, one hiding a tiger and the other a lady he must marry.
forced_question: He will look at me and open the door I point to. Behind one is death, behind the other a woman I hate, who will marry him. What do I signal?

options.A: Point to the lady
options.B: Point to the tiger
options.C: Give no signal
options.D: Point to the lady and leave the kingdom

tradeoff_axis: Possessive love/jealousy vs love's mercy

title: The Open Boat
author: Stephen Crane
plot: Four survivors of a shipwreck row a dinghy toward shore through dangerous surf.
forced_question: The boat is going over. The captain is injured. What do I do?

options.A: Swim straight for shore
options.B: Stay near the captain and help him
options.C: Help the oiler, the strongest swimmer, to lead
options.D: Hold on to the boat with everyone

author_path: Each man swims for himself. The oiler drowns, and the rest are pulled from the surf.
tradeoff_axis: Self-preservation vs solidarity

title: The Three Strangers
author: Thomas Hardy
plot: During a christening party at a remote cottage, a stranger arrives who turns out to be an escaped convict. The hangman due to execute him then arrives too.
stop_anchor: his white lips were parted, and his eyes fixed on the merry officer of justice in the middle of the room.
forced_question: You are the third stranger. You enter a shepherd's party on your way to visit your condemned brother in prison. You recognize your brother, escaped and sitting by the chimney, and the other stranger is singing about hanging a sheep-stealer tomorrow. He is your brother's intended executioner. Neither has identified you to the company. What do you do now?

options.A: Run and say nothing
options.B: Turn him in
options.C: Warn him quietly and help him escape
options.D: Tell the hangman his case is unjust and ask for mercy

author_path: He flees. The searchers chase him instead of the convict, who escapes, and the shepherds quietly let him get away.
tradeoff_axis: Family loyalty vs law/justice

title: The Bet
author: Anton Chekhov
translator: S. S. Koteliansky & J. M. Murry (1915)
plot: A banker bets a young lawyer two million roubles that he cannot endure fifteen years of voluntary solitary confinement. Fifteen years later the banker is ruined, and paying would finish him.
forced_question: I am the banker. Tomorrow at noon I owe this man two million roubles I no longer have; paying means bankruptcy and disgrace. He is asleep and frail in front of me, the watchman is gone, and nobody would suspect me. What do I do?

options.A: Smother him now and let it pass as a natural death; the bet dies with him
options.B: Wake him, confess I am ruined, and beg him to accept a smaller settlement
options.C: Leave quietly and pay in full tomorrow, accepting my ruin as the price of my word
options.D: Leave quietly and, tomorrow, refuse to pay, calling the bet a frivolous drunken wager with no legal force

author_path: He finds a note in which the lawyer renounces the money and plans to leave five hours early. The banker kisses his head, weeps with self-contempt, and goes home. The next day he locks the note in his safe.
tradeoff_axis: Self-preservation and wealth vs. the life of another and keeping one's word

title: Enemies
author: Anton Chekhov
translator: Constance Garnett (1921, The Schoolmaster and Other Stories)
plot: Minutes after his only son dies of diphtheria, the country doctor Kirilov is begged by a wealthy stranger, Abogin, to come at once to his wife, who has collapsed with a heart attack.
forced_question: You are Dr. Kirilov. Your only child has just died and your wife is alone with his body. Abogin says his wife has suddenly become gravely ill, eight or nine miles away, and promises to bring you home within an hour. You have explained your loss, but he continues to plead for your help. What do you do now?

options.A: Go at once; a doctor's duty to a dying patient comes first, whatever my grief
options.B: Refuse and stay with my wife and my dead son; tonight no one has the right to ask this of me
options.C: Refuse to go but give him the name of another doctor and some instructions to pass on
options.D: Agree to go only if he brings his wife here, so I do not leave my wife alone

author_path: Kirilov goes reluctantly. The wife has faked the illness to run off with her lover. Abogin vents his humiliation to Kirilov, the two men trade bitter insults, and Kirilov leaves with a lifelong contempt for the rich.
tradeoff_axis: Professional duty and mercy to a stranger vs. private grief and duty to family

title: The Lady with the Dog
author: Anton Chekhov
plot: Gurov, a married Moscow banker and serial philanderer, has a holiday affair in Yalta with the young married Anna Sergeyevna. He assumes he will forget her, and back in Moscow he finds he cannot.
forced_question: I am Gurov. I have a wife and children in Moscow, and the woman I love is married and lives in a provincial town. If I go there, I could ruin her marriage and reputation and live a double life myself. What do I do?

options.A: Go to S—— to find her, whatever the consequences
options.B: Stay in Moscow and try to let the memory fade, out of duty to my family and hers
options.C: Tell my wife the truth and ask for a separation before I pursue Anna
options.D: Write to Anna and let her decide whether we meet again, rather than turning up unannounced

author_path: He goes to S——, finds her at the theatre, and they begin meeting secretly in Moscow. The story ends with them knowing the hardest part has only just begun.
tradeoff_axis: Marital fidelity and social duty vs. love and authenticity

title: How Much Land Does a Man Need?
author: Leo Tolstoy
plot: Pahom, a land-hungry peasant, gets a deal from the Bashkirs: for 1,000 roubles he can have all the land he walks round between sunrise and sunset, but he loses everything if he is not back at the start by sundown.
forced_question: I am Pahom. I have already marked out a huge piece of land, the best is still ahead, and turning back now means a smaller holding than I dreamed of. I am exhausted and the sun is sinking. What do I do?

options.A: Turn back now on the shortest line and settle for what I have marked
options.B: Mark one more stretch of the best land, then head straight back
options.C: Keep going for as much as I can and race the sun at the end
options.D: Abandon the bargain and walk back slowly; no land is worth risking my life

author_path: He keeps extending the circle and has to run the last stretch. He reaches the starting point as the sun sets and drops dead. His servant buries him in a grave six feet long.
tradeoff_axis: Greed and ambition vs. sufficiency and self-preservation

title: What Men Live By
author: Leo Tolstoy
plot: Simon, a poor shoemaker, is walking home drunk without the sheepskin he went to buy. Behind a roadside shrine he finds a naked stranger freezing in the snow.
forced_question: I am Simon, a poor shoemaker. My wife is waiting at home with nothing to eat, I have failed to bring back the sheepskin, and there is a naked stranger who may be a thief, freezing behind the shrine. What do I do?

options.A: Go back, give him my own coat and boots, and take him home
options.B: Keep walking; I cannot feed my own household and he may be dangerous
options.C: Go back and give him my coat, but send him on to the village rather than bringing him home
options.D: Hurry home and send someone else from the village to deal with him

author_path: Simon turns back, clothes him, and brings him home. His wife Matryona rages, then relents and feeds him. The stranger, Michael, turns out to be an angel learning what men live by.
tradeoff_axis: Charity to a stranger vs. self-protection and duty to one's own household

title: God Sees the Truth, but Does Not Tell at Once
author: Leo Tolstoy
plot: Aksénov, a merchant, is wrongly convicted of a murder and spends 26 years in a Siberian prison. A new convict, Makar Semyonich, turns out to be the real murderer who framed him.
forced_question: You are Aksénov. You have spent twenty-six years in prison for a murder you did not commit. You strongly suspect Makar committed it, but are not certain. You did see him digging an escape tunnel; he threatened you if you told. The prison chief now demands that you identify the digger, who will be severely flogged. What do you do now?

options.A: Name Makar; justice is finally due, and I am asked for the truth
options.B: Say "I cannot say" and protect him, leaving his fate to God
options.C: Name him, but also tell the Governor about the old murder so my own case is reopened
options.D: Stay silent now, and confront Makar privately to demand that he confess the murder

author_path: Aksénov says he will not tell. That night Makar begs his forgiveness and confesses the old murder. Aksénov forgives him and feels at peace. His pardon arrives after he has died.
tradeoff_axis: Justice and honesty vs. mercy and forgiveness of an enemy

title: The Two Old Men
author: Leo Tolstoy
plot: Two old peasants, Efím and Eliséy, set out on foot for Jerusalem. Eliséy stops at a hut for a drink and finds a family dying of famine.
forced_question: I am Eliséy. I promised God and myself this pilgrimage to Jerusalem, and my friend is waiting for me ahead. If I spend my money saving this family I can never make the journey. If I walk on, they will probably die. What do I do?

options.A: Stay, redeem their land, and spend whatever it takes, giving up the pilgrimage
options.B: Leave them food and a little money, then hurry on to catch up with Efím
options.C: Walk on to Jerusalem; I have helped enough and I made a vow to God
options.D: Go to the village elders and the priest to get the community to support them, then continue

author_path: Eliséy stays, redeems their land, buys them a cow and a cart, slips away before dawn, and goes home. Efím reaches Jerusalem but keeps glimpsing Eliséy at the holy places. Back home he learns what Eliséy did.
tradeoff_axis: Religious vow and personal piety vs. concrete mercy to strangers

title: After the Ball ("After the Dance")
author: Leo Tolstoy
translator: Uncredited (The Forged Coupon and Other Stories, ed. C. Hagberg Wright, 1911)
plot: Ivan Vasilievich, deeply in love with Varinka, dances with her all night at a ball where her father, a gallant colonel, charms everyone. At dawn he sees the same colonel supervising the brutal running of the gauntlet by a Tatar deserter.
forced_question: I am Ivan. Last night I loved this family; this morning I watched her father order a man flogged bloody and beat a soldier for going easy. I am expected to propose to his daughter and to make my career in the army or the civil service. What do I do?

options.A: Confront the colonel publicly here and now
options.B: Go on courting Varinka; her father's duty is not her fault, and this is just how the army works
options.C: Quietly withdraw: stop seeing Varinka and give up any service career
options.D: Report the abuse to a higher authority and accept the social cost

author_path: Ivan flees in shame and horror. He cannot face Varinka without seeing her father, so his love fades away, and he never enters military or any other state service.
tradeoff_axis: Love and conformity vs. moral witness and conscience

title: The Mantle ("The Overcoat")
author: Nikolai Gogol
plot: Akaki Akakievitch, a poor and humble copying clerk, scrimps for months to buy a new mantle, which is stolen on its first night out. On advice, he goes to an "important personage" for help.
forced_question: I am a newly promoted high official. A shabby junior clerk has bypassed the proper channels to bring me his stolen-coat problem, and an old friend is in the room watching how I handle subordinates. What do I do?

options.A: Rebuke him sternly for breaching protocol, to keep my authority
options.B: Put my dignity aside, hear him out kindly, and personally push the police to find the coat
options.C: Send him back through the proper channels politely, without humiliating him
options.D: Help him quietly from my own pocket so he can replace the mantle

author_path: The Personage berates him so fiercely that Akaki staggers out, catches a fever and dies. Later the Personage feels remorse, his own cloak is snatched by Akaki's ghost, and he becomes humbler.
tradeoff_axis: Status, hierarchy and pride vs. compassion for the powerless

title: Mumu
author: Ivan Turgenev
translator: Constance Garnett (1897; in Stories by Foreign Authors: Russian, 1898)
plot: Gerasim, a huge deaf-mute serf, rescues and raises a puppy, Mumu, his only companion after his mistress married off the woman he loved. The capricious old lady orders the dog got rid of.
forced_question: I am Gerasim, a serf. My mistress, who owns me, has ordered my dog destroyed; the dog is the only creature that loves me. I have promised the household I will do it myself. What do I do?

options.A: Drown Mumu myself as promised; I owe my mistress obedience
options.B: Secretly give Mumu to someone far away and say it is done
options.C: Take Mumu and run away from the estate, giving up my place
options.D: Refuse openly and defend Mumu, whatever punishment follows

author_path: Gerasim rows out and drowns Mumu himself. Then he walks off the estate and back to his native village, never returns to the lady, and never keeps another dog.
tradeoff_axis: Obedience and promise-keeping vs. love and resistance to unjust authority

title: Biryuk
author: Ivan Turgenev
plot: Foma, a feared and incorruptible forester nicknamed Biryuk ("the wolf"), catches a starving peasant cutting down a birch in his master's woods during a storm.
forced_question: I am Biryuk, the forester. My whole living depends on guarding my master's wood honestly, and everyone hates me for it. A starving peasant I caught red-handed is begging for his children's sake. What do I do?

options.A: Hand him over to the steward as my duty requires
options.B: Let him go and keep quiet about it
options.C: Accept the hunter's money for the tree and let the peasant go
options.D: Let him go, but keep his horse and axe as a penalty

author_path: After the peasant curses him, Biryuk suddenly unties him, shoves the horse at him, says "Get away," and warns the narrator to tell no one.
tradeoff_axis: Duty and integrity in one's office vs. mercy to the desperate

title: The Diamond Necklace ("The Necklace")
author: Guy de Maupassant
translator: A. M. C. McMaster, A. E. Henderson, Mme Quesada et al. (1903)
plot: Mathilde Loisel, a clerk's vain wife, borrows a diamond necklace from her rich friend Mme Forestier for a ministry ball, then loses it.
forced_question: I am Mathilde. I lost my friend's diamond necklace. Replacing it in secret would mean ten years of debt for my husband and me; telling her the truth means humiliation and maybe losing her friendship. What do I do?

options.A: Tell Mme Forestier the truth now and offer to repay her over time
options.B: Secretly buy an identical necklace on loans and return it as if nothing had happened
options.C: Confess the loss and ask her what the necklace was really worth before we take on any debt
options.D: Delay and hope she never asks for it back

author_path: They secretly replace it and spend ten years in grinding poverty paying off the debt. Then Mathilde tells Mme Forestier, who reveals that the original was paste, worth at most 500 francs.
tradeoff_axis: Honesty vs. pride and reputation

title: Two Friends
author: Guy de Maupassant
translator: A. M. C. McMaster, A. E. Henderson, Mme Quesada et al. (1903)
plot: During the siege of Paris, two fishing friends, Morissot and Sauvage, slip past the lines to fish and are captured by Prussians as suspected spies.
forced_question: I am Morissot. If I give the password, my friend and I live and no one will ever know. If I refuse, we are both shot in minutes. What do I do?

options.A: Refuse; I will not betray my country
options.B: Give the password to save both our lives
options.C: Give a false password to buy time
options.D: Ask to speak with Sauvage first so we decide together

author_path: Morissot refuses, and Sauvage refuses too. They are shot and thrown into the river. The officer orders their fish fried for his own meal.
tradeoff_axis: Loyalty to country and honor vs. survival and friendship

title: Mother Sauvage
author: Guy de Maupassant
translator: A. M. C. McMaster, A. E. Henderson, Mme Quesada et al. (1903)
plot: An old peasant widow is made to lodge four young Prussian soldiers, who are kind and help with her chores. Then she gets a letter saying her only son has been killed by the Prussians.
forced_question: I am an old widow. My only son has been cut in two by a Prussian shell. Four young Prussians who have treated me kindly are sleeping under my roof tonight, and they trust me. What do I do?

options.A: Burn the house down with them inside to avenge my son
options.B: Grieve, but do them no harm; they did not kill my son
options.C: Throw them out of my house and refuse to serve them
options.D: Report my grief to their officer and ask to be freed from lodging enemy soldiers

author_path: She asks their names and their families' addresses, then sets the house on fire with them in the loft and confesses calmly to the Prussians, who shoot her.
tradeoff_axis: Vengeance and grief vs. mercy toward individual enemies

title: El Verdugo
author: Honoré de Balzac
plot: In Napoleonic Spain, the Marquis de Léganès's family is condemned for a revolt against the French garrison. The French general offers to spare one son, to carry on the family name, if that son executes the rest.
focal_character: Juanito, eldest son of the Marquis
forced_question: I am Juanito. My father orders me to survive by executing my whole family myself, so that our name does not die. If I refuse, every one of us is killed. What do I do?

options.A: Obey my father and become the executioner
options.B: Refuse and die with my family
options.C: Ask to die in place of one of my siblings, though the bargain does not allow it
options.D: Beg the French commander for different terms, refusing to act until he answers

author_path: Juanito obeys and executes his father and siblings. His mother throws herself from the rock before he can strike her. He lives on as "El Verdugo" (the executioner), carrying the family name and wishing he were dead.
tradeoff_axis: Filial obedience and lineage vs. personal conscience and refusal to kill kin

title: La Grande Bretèche
author: Honoré de Balzac
plot: M. de Merret comes home unexpectedly and suspects that his wife's Spanish lover, Bagos de Férédia, is hiding in her closet. She swears on a crucifix that no one is there.
forced_question: I am M. de Merret. My wife has sworn on the cross that there is no one in her closet. I am almost certain she is lying. Opening it would expose her and destroy our marriage; not opening it means living with the doubt. What do I do?

options.A: Open the closet and confront whatever I find
options.B: Accept her oath publicly and never open it
options.C: Have the closet door walled up, taking her at her word but making sure
options.D: Leave the house and seek a separation without forcing the question

author_path: He has Gorenflot wall up the closet door, with the lover alive inside, and stays in the room for twenty days until no sound remains.
tradeoff_axis: Honor, jealousy and vengeance vs. trust, mercy and the sanctity of an oath

title: An Episode under the Terror
author: Honoré de Balzac
plot: In 1793, a non-juring priest is hiding in a Paris garret with two nuns. A mysterious stranger comes and begs him to say a secret mass for the soul of the guillotined Louis XVI.
forced_question: I am a hunted priest. A stranger I cannot identify asks me to say a forbidden mass for the executed king, and to keep it secret. If he is an informer, the two nuns and I will go to the guillotine. If he is sincere, refusing would betray my vocation. What do I do?

options.A: Say the mass tonight, trusting God and the man's sincerity
options.B: Refuse; I cannot risk the lives of the nuns
options.C: Agree only if he first reveals who he is and why he asks
options.D: Pray for the king privately but not with him present

author_path: The abbé says the mass. The stranger returns each year with gifts, and on the anniversary of the execution the abbé learns he is Sanson, the executioner who beheaded the king, seeking absolution.
tradeoff_axis: Religious duty and compassion vs. prudence and protecting others

title: Mateo Falcone
author: Prosper Mérimée
plot: Mateo, a feared Corsican with a strict code of honor, comes home to learn that his ten-year-old son Fortunato hid a wounded outlaw and then betrayed him to the soldiers for a silver watch.
forced_question: I am Mateo. My only son has broken the most sacred rule of our people by betraying a man under our roof for a bribe, and he has shamed our house forever. He is ten years old. What do I do?

options.A: Execute my son to wash out the dishonor
options.B: Beat him severely and send him away to be raised elsewhere
options.C: Forgive him as a child and bear the family's disgrace
options.D: Go after the soldiers and try to free Gianetto to restore our honor

author_path: Mateo takes Fortunato into a ravine, makes him say his prayers, and shoots him dead. Then he arranges for his son-in-law to come and live with them as heir.
tradeoff_axis: Honor code and loyalty vs. paternal love and mercy

title: The Little Mermaid
author: Hans Christian Andersen
plot: A mermaid trades her voice for legs to win a prince's love and an immortal soul, and she will die if he marries another. He marries a princess instead.
forced_question: I am the little mermaid. The man I love is asleep beside his bride. If I kill him with this knife before dawn, I live; if not, I turn into sea foam. What do I do?

options.A: Kill the prince and return to the sea
options.B: Throw the knife away and accept my death
options.C: Wake him and tell him the truth, though I have no voice
options.D: Run away and use my last hours however I can

author_path: She kisses the bride's forehead, throws the knife into the sea, and leaps in herself. Instead of dissolving into foam she becomes a daughter of the air, able to earn an immortal soul.
tradeoff_axis: Self-preservation vs. selfless love and the sanctity of others' lives

title: The Emperor's New Clothes
author: Hans Christian Andersen
plot: Two swindlers claim to weave cloth that is invisible to anyone unfit for office or very stupid. The emperor sends his honest old minister to inspect the work.
forced_question: I am the emperor's most trusted old minister. I see nothing on the looms. Saying so may brand me unfit for my office; praising it would deceive my emperor. What do I do?

options.A: Say plainly that I see nothing
options.B: Praise the cloth to protect my position
options.C: Say nothing yet and quietly ask others what they see
options.D: Report privately to the emperor that something seems wrong, without accusing anyone

author_path: He praises the pattern and colors and reports favorably to the emperor. The deception spreads until a child at the procession says, "But he has nothing on!"
tradeoff_axis: Honesty and courage vs. self-interest and conformity

title: The Postmaster
author: Rabindranath Tagore
translator: Uncredited (Stories from Tagore, Macmillan 1918, revised from the 1916 Hungry Stones / Mashi translations)
plot: A lonely Calcutta postmaster in a remote village is cared for by the orphan Ratan. His request for a transfer is refused; he resigns and prepares to leave.
stop_anchor: "Dada, will you take me to your home?"
forced_question: You are the postmaster. After your request for a transfer was refused, you resigned and told Ratan you are going home. This orphan girl has cared for you during illness, and you have taught her to read. She now asks whether you will take her home with you. What do you do now?

options.A: Take her with me and arrange for her care
options.B: Laugh it off and leave, giving her some money
options.C: Ask my successor to look after her before I go
options.D: Postpone my departure until I have found her a proper guardian

author_path: He laughs, says "What an idea!", asks his successor to be kind to her, and offers her money, which she refuses. He leaves by boat and reasons his pang away. Ratan keeps waiting for him to return.
tradeoff_axis: Personal obligation and compassion vs. convenience and social distance

title: The Cabuliwallah
author: Rabindranath Tagore
translator: Translated by several hands, incl. C. F. Andrews (The Hungry Stones and Other Stories, 1916)
plot: A Calcutta writer's little daughter Mini befriends Rahmun, an Afghan fruit-seller who misses his own daughter. Rahmun is jailed for years after stabbing a debtor.
forced_question: I am Mini's father. On my daughter's wedding day a former convict, once her dear friend, asks to see her. It is inauspicious, and his visit might upset the ceremony and the in-laws. What do I do?

options.A: Send him away; today is not the day
options.B: Let him see Mini briefly
options.C: Let him see her and give him money from the wedding funds so he can go home to his own daughter
options.D: Promise him a visit after the wedding but turn him away now

author_path: The father first refuses, then sees the handprint of Rahmun's own daughter that he carries. He calls Mini, gives Rahmun money to go home, and cuts back the wedding lights and band, so the feast is less bright but kinder.
tradeoff_axis: Propriety and family honor vs. compassion and shared humanity

title: The Queen of Spades
author: Alexander Pushkin
plot: Hermann, a poor and ambitious officer, becomes obsessed with an old countess said to know a secret of three winning cards. He gets into her house through her young ward Lizaveta.
forced_question: I am Hermann. This frail old woman holds the secret that would make my fortune and refuses to give it to me. I have deceived a girl to get in here and I have a pistol. What do I do?

options.A: Threaten her with the pistol to force the secret
options.B: Leave now and give up the scheme
options.C: Kneel and plead with her, offering to take her sin on my own soul
options.D: Confess everything to Lizaveta and end the deception

author_path: Hermann pleads, then draws an unloaded pistol, and the countess dies of fright. Her ghost later gives him the cards, but on the third night he wins with the wrong card, the queen of spades, and goes mad.
tradeoff_axis: Ambition and greed vs. respect for others and honesty

title: The Shot
author: Alexander Pushkin
plot: Years ago a carefree Count fired first in a duel with Silvio and missed, then ate cherries while facing Silvio's pistol, so Silvio kept his shot in reserve. Now the Count is happily married, and Silvio has come for him.
forced_question: I am Silvio. For six years I have waited to take my shot at the man who mocked death when he faced me. Now he has everything to lose and his wife is begging me. What do I do?

options.A: Fire at the Count as I am entitled to
options.B: Spare him; seeing his fear is satisfaction enough
options.C: Insist on a new duel by lots, then decide
options.D: Walk away without firing and release the debt

author_path: Silvio makes them draw lots again; the Count fires and misses into a painting. Silvio, content to have seen the Count afraid, fires into the same picture and leaves. He later dies fighting for Greek independence.
tradeoff_axis: Honor and revenge vs. mercy

title: The Dream of a Ridiculous Man
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
plot: A man convinced that nothing matters has decided to shoot himself tonight. On the way home, a terrified little girl grabs his sleeve and begs him to help her dying mother.
forced_question: I believe nothing matters and I intend to die tonight. A child is begging me to help her mother. If nothing matters, why should I care? Yet I feel I should. What do I do?

options.A: Go with her and help her mother
options.B: Shout at her and drive her off; nothing matters
options.C: Send her to a policeman or neighbor and go home
options.D: Help her and reconsider my plan to die

author_path: He stamps and shouts at her and she runs away. At home he dozes off over his revolver and dreams of an innocent world that he corrupts. He wakes changed, preaching love, and goes to look for the girl.
tradeoff_axis: Nihilism and self-absorption vs. duty and compassion to others
